title: Dynamic Scheduling and Out-of-Order Execution
subtitle: Why a modern CPU does not run your program in the order you wrote it.

objectives: Explain why a processor may execute instructions out of program order
Define dynamic scheduling and reservation stations
Follow a simplified Tomasulo algorithm: issue, execute, write result on the CDB
Explain register renaming and which dependences it removes
Compare in-order and out-of-order execution with cycle counts

steps.question: Your program says A, then B, then C. Why might the CPU finish C before B?
clues: A slow instruction (a divide, a cache miss) makes its **dependents** wait.
Instructions that do **not** depend on it can run **in the meantime**.
The CPU just has to make the **result look as if** it ran in order.

notes.explain: Let students guess before revealing the clues.
Read the objectives aloud; they return in the learning report.

steps.title: In-order execution waits behind the slowest

blocks.text: In an **in-order** machine an instruction cannot start before the ones before it. If the first one is slow and the second depends on it, **everything behind them waits**, even instructions that have nothing to do with the divide.

steps.why: The last two instructions are independent, yet an in-order processor makes them wait for the divide.
steps.real: A cache miss or a divide can leave a simple in-order core idle for dozens of cycles.

explainAgain.beginner: A queue at the bank: the person at the front is slow, and everyone behind has to wait even if they only want to ask a quick question at another window.

steps.title: Try it: in order or out of order

blocks.title: div, dependent add, two independent instructions
blocks.hint: Switch **Execution order** between In order and Out of order, and try widths 1 and 2.

steps.why: In order: 14 cycles (width 1) or 13 (width 2). Out of order: 12 cycles either way: sub and and finish early, then the dependent add finishes last.

steps.question: On a 1-wide machine, how many cycles does the div/add/sub/and sequence take out of order (in order it takes 14)?

reveal.text: The long chain **div (8 cycles) then add** sets the minimum: the add writes in cycle 12. The independent sub and and finish earlier, in cycles 5 and 6. Total **12**.

steps.result: The critical path is the dependent chain, not the number of instructions.

steps.title: Out of order, but still correct

items: Instructions that depend on each other are **never** reordered past a dependence
Independent instructions can run in any order without changing the result
The processor **commits** (makes visible) results **in program order**, so the program behaves as if it ran in order
This is why a modern core can run instructions out of order and still be correct

steps.why: Reordering is allowed only because the observable result is the same as in order.
steps.real: Programmers never see the reordering; debuggers show the program as written.

mistake.wrong: Out-of-order execution can change what a single program computes.
mistake.right: It cannot: true dependences are respected and results are committed in order.

steps.statement: An out-of-order processor may produce a different final result than an in-order one.
steps.why: Dependences are respected and results are committed in program order.

steps.question: What is out-of-order execution for?
options: To let independent instructions run while a slow one is waiting
To reduce the number of registers
steps.why: It uses the time an in-order processor wastes waiting.
feedback: The result must stay the same.

steps.title: Dynamic scheduling

head: Static scheduling
Dynamic scheduling
rows: The hardware, while the program runs
Only what the compiler can predict
Run-time delays such as cache misses
Needs recompiling for a new machine
Old code runs faster on new hardware
A lot of hardware (queues, tags, buses)

steps.why: The hardware sees delays the compiler cannot predict. A load that misses the cache takes far longer than a load that hits, and the schedule adapts.
steps.real: Almost every laptop, phone and server core uses dynamic scheduling.

steps.title: A load that misses the cache

blocks.title: lw takes 6 cycles (a miss)
blocks.hint: Switch to Out of order: the three independent instructions run during the miss.

steps.why: In order: 13 cycles (width 1) or 11 (width 2). Out of order: 10 cycles in both.

steps.title: Reservation stations

items: A **reservation station** is a small buffer in front of an execution unit
It holds an **instruction**, its **operand values** if ready, or **tags** naming the unit that will produce them
The instruction **starts when all operands are ready**, regardless of program order
A tag is just a name for "the result that will come from that station"

head: Field
Meaning
rows: Which station will produce an operand that is not ready

steps.why: Reservation stations let instructions wait for operands without blocking the ones behind them.
steps.real: Intel and AMD cores call their versions the scheduler or issue queue.

explainAgain.beginner: A to-do list for each worker: every task lists what is still missing, and it can be started as soon as the missing parts arrive.

deeper.text: In real designs the stations are part of a larger structure that also includes a reorder buffer, which commits results in order.

steps.prompt: Put the life of an instruction in a reservation-station machine in order.
items: Issue: placed in a station in program order
Wait until all operands are ready
Execute in a functional unit

steps.why: The instruction waits for operands, runs, then broadcasts the result.

steps.title: Mini challenge
steps.prompt: Match each term with its meaning.

pairs.b: Buffer holding an instruction and its operands or tags
A name for a result that is still being computed
Reordering by the hardware at run time
Sending an instruction to a station, in program order

steps.why: These four terms are the vocabulary of Tomasulo's algorithm.

steps.title: Find the mistake
steps.prompt: One statement about dynamic scheduling is wrong. Click it.
lines: 1. The hardware decides the execution order while the program runs.
2. A reservation station can hold an operand tag instead of a value.
3. An instruction must wait until all earlier instructions have finished.
4. It lets independent instructions run during a cache miss.
steps.explain: An instruction only waits for its own operands, not for every earlier instruction.
steps.fix: It waits for its operands only.

steps.title: Three steps (simplified)

head: Step
What happens
rows: Take the next instruction; put it in a free reservation station of the right kind; copy ready operand values or the tags of the stations that will produce them; mark its destination register with its own tag
When both operands are ready and the unit is free, the instruction starts
The unit broadcasts **tag + value** on the common data bus (CDB); every waiting station and the registers that were waiting for that tag capture the value

blocks.text: We keep it simple: no memory, no branches, no reorder buffer. The goal is to see why instructions can run out of order, not to learn every detail.

steps.why: Only these three steps are needed to understand how dependences are tracked at run time.
steps.real: IBM introduced this scheme in 1967 for the floating-point unit of the System/360 Model 91; Tomasulo's idea is inside today's CPUs.

notes.explain: Issue is in order; execute and write result are out of order.

steps.title: Build the organisation

steps.text: Instructions are **issued in program order** from a queue. Each goes to the reservation station of the unit it needs.

A **reservation station** holds an instruction and its operands (or **tags** for operands still being computed). It sends the instruction to the unit **as soon as its operands are ready**, whatever the order.
When a unit finishes, it puts the **result and its tag on the common data bus (CDB)**. Every waiting station listens and picks up the value it needs.
The registers also take the result, and a register that is still being computed holds a **tag** instead of a value: this is **register renaming**.

steps.why: The CDB is what lets one result reach every waiting instruction at the same time.

steps.question: In the run you are about to see (div r1; add r4,r1,r5; sub r6,r7,r8), which of add and sub finishes first?
options: sub: it does not depend on the div

reveal.text: The add waits for r1 from the divide (cycle 10) and finishes in cycle 12. The independent sub finishes in cycle **5**, out of program order.

steps.result: Watch the tag DIV travel on the CDB to the waiting add.

steps.title: Follow div, add and sub

steps.text: The complete organisation. Press Play or Step to follow div, add and sub.
**Cycle 1: issue div r1,r2,r3.** Its operands are ready, so it waits in a Mul/Div station.
**Cycles 2 to 9: the div executes** (it takes 8 cycles). The register r1 is marked "result coming from the divider".
**Cycle 2: issue add r4,r1,r5.** r1 is not ready: the station stores the **tag DIV** instead of a value and waits.
**Cycle 3: issue sub r6,r7,r8.** Its operands are ready, so it runs in the adder **ahead of the waiting add**: this is out-of-order execution. It writes its result in cycle 5.
**Cycle 10: the div writes r1 on the CDB.** The waiting add captures the value (it was listening for the tag DIV).
**Cycles 11 and 12: the add executes and writes r4.** Total 12 cycles; an in-order machine would have taken 14.

steps.why: Step through all six events: the sub overtakes the waiting add, and the add starts only when the CDB carries the div result.

steps.question: What does the common data bus carry?
options: A result together with its tag
steps.why: It broadcasts the result and the tag of the station that produced it.
feedback: Instructions travel from the queue to the stations.
Memory is not part of this simplified model.

steps.question: In which step are instructions still handled in program order?
steps.why: Issue is in order; execute and write result are not.
feedback: Execute starts when operands are ready.
Write result happens when a unit finishes.

questions.q: What does a reservation station hold when an operand is not ready?
questions.a: The tag of the station that will produce it.

questions.q: How does a waiting instruction get its operand?
questions.a: By listening to the CDB for its tag.

steps.title: Name dependences

head: Instruction
Problem
rows: Reads r5 from 3 and r1 from 4 (true RAW)

steps.why: Instructions 3 and 4 do not use any value from the earlier instructions, they only reuse their register names. Without renaming they must wait.
steps.real: A compiler has only 32 registers to name thousands of values, so names are reused constantly.

mistake.wrong: WAR and WAW are real data flow and cannot be avoided.
mistake.right: They are only name clashes. Giving each result a new name removes them.

steps.title: Renaming gives every result a new name

left.title: Before renaming
items: `div r1,r2,r3`
`add r4,r1,r5`
`sub r5,r6,r7`
`or r1,r8,r9`
`and r10,r5,r1`

right.title: After renaming (every result gets a new name)
items: `div T1,r2,r3`
`add T2,T1,r5`
`sub T3,r6,r7`
`or T4,r8,r9`
`and T5,T3,T4`

steps.why: Only the **true** dependences remain: add needs T1, and needs T3 and T4. The WAR and WAW dependences are gone.
steps.real: Real processors have far more physical registers (100 or more) than the 32 architectural ones in the instruction set.

steps.title: Try it: renaming on and off

blocks.title: div, add, sub, or, and (name dependences)
blocks.hint: Compare In order, Out of order without renaming and Out of order with renaming.

steps.why: In order: 16 cycles. Out of order without renaming: 14 (the sub and or must wait for the older instructions to read and write r5 and r1). Out of order with renaming: 12.

steps.question: Out of order on a 1-wide machine, how many cycles does renaming save in this example (without renaming it takes 14)?

reveal.text: Without renaming: 14 cycles. With renaming: **12** cycles. The sub and or no longer wait for the earlier instructions to finish reading and writing the old names.

steps.result: In order the same code needs 16.

steps.title: Committing in order (idea only)

items: Results may finish out of order, but they become **visible** in program order
A **reorder buffer** holds finished results until all older instructions have finished
If an older instruction faults or a branch was mispredicted, the younger results are simply **discarded**
This gives precise exceptions: the program looks as if it stopped exactly at the faulting instruction

steps.why: Out-of-order execution and in-order commit together give speed with the right answer.
steps.real: This is how a CPU can run past a branch before knowing the direction (Class 16).

steps.title: Think, pair, share
steps.prompt: Why do processors have more physical registers than the 32 the instruction set can name?
steps.answer: The extra physical registers are the new names used by renaming: each in-flight result gets its own register, which removes WAR and WAW dependences. The instruction set still names only 32 registers (code size and compatibility), while the hardware maps them to many physical registers.

steps.title: Discussion
steps.question: Out-of-order execution speeds programs up but costs hardware and power. When is it worth it?
ideas: Programs with unpredictable delays (cache misses) gain a lot.
Programs full of dependent chains gain little: the chain sets the time.
Low-power chips (watches, sensors) often keep simple in-order cores to save energy.
Servers and laptops usually choose out-of-order for single-thread speed.

steps.question: What is a reservation station?
steps.answer: A buffer that holds an instruction and its operands (or tags) until all operands are ready.
steps.solution: It lets instructions wait for operands without blocking the ones behind them.

steps.question: div r1 (8 cycles), add r4,r1,r5, sub r6,r7,r8, and r9,r10,r11 on a 1-wide machine: how many cycles in order and out of order?
steps.answer: 14 cycles in order; 12 out of order.
steps.solution: In order the sub and and wait behind the add. Out of order they finish in cycles 5 and 6 and the add (cycle 12) finishes last.
steps.hint: The longest chain is div then add.

steps.question: In the Tomasulo run, in which cycle does the add start executing, and why not earlier?
steps.answer: Cycle 11: it needs r1, which the div writes on the CDB in cycle 10.
steps.solution: The add's station holds the tag DIV until the broadcast arrives, so it cannot start before cycle 11.
steps.hint: When does the divide write its result?
steps.mistake: Saying the add starts as soon as it is issued.

steps.question: Sequence: div r1,r2,r3 (8 cycles); add r4,r1,r5; sub r5,r6,r7; or r1,r8,r9; and r10,r5,r1. Give the cycles in order, out of order without renaming, and out of order with renaming (1-wide).
steps.answer: In order 16; out of order without renaming 14; with renaming 12.
steps.solution: In order everything is serialised behind the divide. Without renaming the sub and or have to respect the WAR and WAW name dependences; with renaming only true dependences remain.
steps.mistake: Believing renaming removes the true dependences too.
steps.title: Exam practice: cycle counting

steps.question: lw r1 (6 cycles, a miss); add r2,r1,r3; sub r4,r5,r6; or r7,r8,r9; xor r11,r12,r13. Give the cycles in order and out of order on a 1-wide machine.
steps.solution: Out of order the three independent instructions run during the miss, so the total is set by the load and its dependent add.
steps.title: Exam practice: cache miss

steps.question: Write the three Tomasulo steps and say which are in program order.
steps.answer: Issue (in order): put the instruction in a station, copy operands or tags. Execute (out of order): start when operands are ready. Write result: broadcast tag and value on the CDB so waiting stations and registers capture it.
steps.mistake: Saying execution also follows program order.
steps.title: Exam practice: tracing

steps.question: Explain why out-of-order execution does not change the result of a program.
steps.answer: Instructions that depend on each other are never reordered past the dependence (true dependences are tracked with tags), the instructions that are reordered are independent, and the results are committed in program order, so the visible state is always as if the program ran in order.
steps.solution: A strong answer names true dependences and in-order commit.
steps.mistake: Saying the processor just guesses and fixes errors later without mentioning dependences.
steps.title: Exam practice: conceptual
What you should remember
remember: In-order execution makes independent instructions wait behind a slow one.
Dynamic scheduling lets the hardware start instructions when their operands are ready.
Reservation stations hold instructions with operand values or tags.
Tomasulo: issue (in order), execute (out of order), write result on the CDB (tag + value).
Register renaming gives each result a new name, which removes WAR and WAW dependences.
Results are committed in program order, so the answer never changes.

mistakes.wrong: Out-of-order execution can change the result.
mistakes.right: Dependences are respected and results are committed in order.

mistakes.wrong: WAR and WAW are real data flow.
mistakes.right: They are name clashes that renaming removes.

mistakes.wrong: Every stage is out of order.

mistakes.right: A dependent chain sets the time; gains depend on independent work.

steps.title: One-minute summary
steps.summary: Dynamic scheduling lets hardware run independent instructions while a slow one waits. Instructions sit in reservation stations until their operands (values or tags) arrive on the common data bus. Issue is in order, execution and write result are out of order, and renaming removes name dependences. Results are committed in program order, so the program still behaves as written.
